summary: Exactly one `["t","scrutiny-fabric"]` tag.
text: Every SCRUTINY event MUST carry exactly one `["t","scrutiny-fabric"]` tag.

summary: Exactly one version `t` tag matching `^scrutiny-v\d+\.\d+\.\d+$`.
text: Every SCRUTINY event MUST carry exactly one version `t` tag matching `^scrutiny-v\d+\.\d+\.\d+$`.

summary: Exactly one event-type `t` tag from the recognised set.
text: Every SCRUTINY event MUST carry exactly one event-type `t` tag from `{scrutiny-product, scrutiny-metadata, scrutiny-binding, scrutiny-patch}`.

summary: Tag names use kebab-case.
text: Tag names use kebab-case; underscored variants from older drafts are not recognised.

summary: Unknown tags MUST be ignored.
text: Unknown tags MUST be ignored by parsers.

summary: Version tags order per-field by digit string (leading zeros ignored; greater length, then lexicographic); never host-number conversion, never whole-tag lexicographic.
text: Ordering between two version tags is a per-field numeric tuple comparison of `(MAJOR, MINOR, PATCH)`. Each field compares as a decimal digit string — leading zeros ignored, the longer string the greater, equal lengths lexicographically — never by conversion to a host number type, and never as a lexicographic comparison of the whole tag value.

summary: Higher-version events MAY be admitted opaquely if V-valid.
text: A higher-version event MAY be admitted opaquely if it satisfies every Validity invariant of this specification.

summary: Higher-version events violating Validity MUST NOT render.
text: A higher-version event that violates a Validity invariant of this specification MUST NOT be rendered as a Product, Metadata, Binding, or Patch.

summary: MUST NOT reject higher-version events *solely* for the version tag.
text: Implementations MUST NOT reject higher-version events *solely* because of the version tag.

summary: OTS is audit signal only; not used for chain construction or tip selection.
text: OpenTimestamps attestations are an audit signal only: consumers MUST NOT use OTS-derived timestamps in canonical-chain construction, overlay classification, or self-fork resolution.

summary: Every consumed event MUST have both its signature and its `id` verified before processing.
text: Before processing any event — including kind 5 deletions and kind 1040 attestations — implementations MUST verify the signature **and** that `id` equals the SHA-256 of the NIP-01 canonical serialization. A signature-only check is insufficient.

summary: `created_at` SHOULD NOT be backdated to a historical date; historical dates belong in `content`.
text: Publishers SHOULD NOT backdate `created_at` to a historical date the event describes. Deployed relays reject events outside a bounded timestamp window; historical dates belong in `content`.

summary: Product `content` field is required.
text: A Product event MUST carry a `content` field (any UTF-8 byte sequence; format is free-form).

summary: Product SHOULD carry ≤64 `i` tags.
text: A Product event SHOULD carry no more than 64 `i` tags.

summary: Product SHOULD carry ≤64 `k` tags.
text: A Product event SHOULD carry no more than 64 `k` tags.

summary: `k` SHOULD contain ≥1 entry per distinct `i` prefix; absence does not invalidate; treat as set.
text: The `k` collection SHOULD contain at minimum one entry per **distinct** `i` prefix kind present in the event. A missing or incomplete `k` collection does NOT invalidate the event; consumers MAY derive the kind from the `i` value's prefix (§9). Consumers MUST treat `k` as a set.

summary: `imeta` attachments OPTIONAL.
text: `imeta` attachments are OPTIONAL.

summary: Metadata `content` field is required.
text: A Metadata event MUST carry a `content` field (any UTF-8 byte sequence; format is free-form).

summary: Metadata SHOULD carry ≤64 `i` tags.
text: A Metadata event SHOULD carry no more than 64 `i` tags.

summary: Metadata SHOULD carry ≤64 `k` tags.
text: A Metadata event SHOULD carry no more than 64 `k` tags.

summary: `k` SHOULD contain ≥1 entry per distinct `i` prefix; absence does not invalidate; treat as set.
text: The `k` collection SHOULD contain at minimum one entry per **distinct** `i` prefix kind present in the event. A missing or incomplete `k` collection does NOT invalidate the event; consumers MAY derive the kind from the `i` value's prefix (§9). Consumers MUST treat `k` as a set.

summary: `imeta` attachments OPTIONAL.
text: `imeta` attachments are OPTIONAL.

summary: Exactly one `e root` tag.
text: A Binding event MUST carry exactly one `e` tag with marker `root`.

summary: Exactly one `e link` tag.
text: A Binding event MUST carry exactly one `e` tag with marker `link`.

summary: `e root` endpoint MUST be a `scrutiny-product`.
text: The `e root` endpoint MUST be a `scrutiny-product` event.

summary: `e link` endpoint MUST be a `scrutiny-metadata`.
text: The `e link` endpoint MUST be a `scrutiny-metadata` event.

summary: Binding with invalid endpoint typing MUST NOT be admitted.
text: A Binding whose endpoints, once observed, do not satisfy BD-3/BD-4 is an invalid SCRUTINY event and MUST NOT be admitted.

summary: Binding with unobserved endpoints is pending; admitted but not rendered.
text: A Binding whose endpoints are not yet observed MUST be treated as *pending*: admitted to local storage but NOT rendered until both endpoints are observed.

summary: Endpoint contradiction → permanently invalid; SHOULD cache rejection.
text: A Binding whose observed endpoint contradicts BD-3/BD-4 transitions to permanently invalid; implementations SHOULD cache the rejection.

summary: Relay-hint advisory; MUST fall back to full relay set if not found on hint.
text: The `<relay>` field in `e` tags is advisory. An empty string means "no hint." Implementations MUST NOT rely on relay hints exclusively and SHOULD query their configured relay set for referenced events; they MUST fall back to their full relay set if the event is not found on the hinted relay.

summary: No patch-based Binding update; correct via kind 5 + replacement.
text: Bindings have no patch-based update mechanism. To correct a Binding, kind 5 delete it and publish a replacement. Patch events cannot target a Binding.

summary: Binding MUST NOT contain more than one `e root` or `e link`.
text: A Binding MUST NOT contain more than one `e root` or more than one `e link`.

summary: Duplicate Binding collapse is a presentation concern.
text: Duplicate detection is a presentation concern. Implementations MAY collapse visually-identical bindings (same root, same link, same pubkey) at render time.

summary: Author-hint mismatch does NOT invalidate the referencing Binding.
text: A mismatch between the author-hint suffix in an `e` tag and the actual event `pubkey` does not invalidate the referencing Binding. Trust decisions MUST be based on the verified event pubkey, not the hint.

summary: Exactly one `e root` tag.
text: A Patch event MUST carry exactly one `e` tag with marker `root` (pointing at the root Product or Metadata).

summary: Exactly one `e reply` tag.
text: A Patch event MUST carry exactly one `e` tag with marker `reply` (pointing at its immediate target).

summary: Zero or one fenced `diff` / `patch` block.
text: A Patch event MUST carry zero or one fenced `diff` / `patch` code block.

summary: Multiple fenced blocks → only the first is the payload.
text: If multiple fenced `diff` / `patch` blocks appear, only the first (document order) is the patch payload; subsequent blocks MUST be treated as prose.

summary: Root-author vs foreign classification by `pubkey`.
text: Authorship classification: a **root-author patch** has `pubkey` equal to the root event's `pubkey`; a **foreign patch** does not.

summary: Root-author patch `e reply` MUST point at root or root-author patch (otherwise ignored for chain); unevaluable while the target is unobserved — held per UR-4.
text: A root-author patch's `e reply` MUST point at the root event or another root-author patch. A root-author patch replying to a foreign patch is ignored for canonical-chain construction (§7.3). While the target is unobserved this rule cannot be evaluated — the parent's authorship class is unknown — so the patch is neither admitted to nor excluded from the chain on its basis; it is retained and held per §7.6 (UR-4).

summary: Foreign patch `e reply` MUST point at root or root-author patch; no overlay-to-overlay.
text: A foreign patch's `e reply` MUST point at the root event or a root-author patch. Overlay-to-overlay reply is invalid (§7.3).

summary: No-op patch participates in chain topology but contributes no change.
text: A no-op patch (no fenced block, or header-only fenced block per §5.2 N1/N2) participates in chain topology but contributes no content change.

summary: Patches append-only; removal only via author's own kind 5.
text: Patches are append-only. A patch cannot be inserted between two existing patches, and its parent pointer cannot be changed after publication. Removal is only via kind 5 deletion by the patch's own author (§10).

summary: `e root` MUST reference a `scrutiny-product` or `scrutiny-metadata` event.
text: The event referenced by `e root` MUST be a `scrutiny-product` or `scrutiny-metadata` event.

summary: Patch with an observed `e root` violating PT-10 MUST NOT be admitted.
text: A Patch whose OBSERVED `e root` violates PT-10 is invalid and MUST NOT be admitted.

summary: Publishers SHOULD include canonical `i` tags for top-level indexers.
text: Publishers SHOULD include canonical `i` tags for top-level indexers the event is *about* (CVE, CPE, PURL, CC certificate ID, FIPS validation number, etc.).

summary: Events SHOULD carry ≤64 `i` tags.
text: Events SHOULD contain no more than 64 `i` tags.

summary: `i` and `k` tags on root events are immutable.
text: `i` tags and `k` tags on root events (Products and Metadata) are immutable. Patches only modify `content` (§4.4). To add or change indexers after publication, publish a new root event.

summary: Deeply nested indexers SHOULD NOT be duplicated as `i` tags.
text: Deeply nested indexers from payload contents (e.g., every component in a large SBOM) SHOULD NOT be duplicated as `i` tags.

summary: SHOULD verify `x` hash by streaming and comparing SHA-256.
text: Implementations SHOULD verify the `x` hash by streaming the artifact contents and comparing against the declared SHA-256.

summary: `size` mismatch is a verification failure equal to hash mismatch.
text: If a declared `size` is present, implementations SHOULD additionally compare fetched byte length against `size` and treat a mismatch as a verification failure of the same severity as a hash mismatch.

summary: Multi-URL `imeta`: first hash-matching mirror is accepted; mirror choice MUST NOT influence validity.
text: A single `imeta` tag MAY carry multiple `url` entries. Implementations SHOULD try them in order and accept the first whose fetched bytes match the declared `x` hash. Mirror selection MUST NOT influence the validity decision — only the hash check does.

summary: MUST warn before displaying unverified artifacts.
text: Implementations MUST warn before displaying or processing unverified artifacts.

summary: `imeta` attachments not required to be referenced in `content`.
text: SCRUTINY extends NIP-92: `imeta` attachments are not required to be referenced in the event's `content` field.

summary: `content` consumed verbatim; no normalization before diff/apply.
text: The `content` field is consumed verbatim as a UTF-8 byte sequence; no normalization (line-ending, trailing-newline, BOM-stripping, whitespace trimming) is performed before diffing or applying.

summary: Consumers MUST NOT normalize patch payload bytes before applying.
text: Consumers MUST NOT normalize the patch-payload byte sequence (the bytes strictly between the fence lines — or, for an unclosed block, after the opening fence line to the end of `content` — each terminated by `\n`) before feeding it to a unified-diff applier.

summary: Backtick-fenced code block; tilde fences not recognised.
text: The patch payload MUST be wrapped in a CommonMark §4.5 fenced code block using backtick (`` ` ``) fences. Tilde (`~`) fences are not recognized as SCRUTINY patch payloads.

summary: Opening fence ≥3 backticks; info string first token `diff` or `patch`.
text: The opening fence MUST consist of three or more consecutive backticks, followed by an info string whose first whitespace-delimited token, lowercased, is `diff` or `patch`. Any additional info-string tokens after the first are ignored.

summary: Closing fence ≥ opening-fence length, when one exists; an unclosed block is a valid code block running to the end of `content`.
text: The closing fence MUST consist of at least as many backticks as the opening fence, on a line of its own (CommonMark §4.5 closing-fence rule).

summary: Variable-length fences: `max(3, N+1)`; a producer obligation, unobservable to a consumer.
text: **Variable-length fences.** Producers MUST choose an opening-fence length of `max(3, N + 1)`, where `N` is the longest run of consecutive backticks anywhere inside the payload bytes. This guarantees that any payload — including patches whose hunks operate on content that itself contains backtick fences (e.g., a Metadata event embedding a code-block PoC) — can be embedded unambiguously. This is a producer obligation, enforced when building an event: a consumer cannot observe a violation, because a payload whose backtick run reached the fence length would have closed the block early (E3) and the bytes after it are not part of the payload at all (E5). There is nothing left for a consumer to check.

summary: Payload = bytes between fence lines, each terminated by `\n`.
text: The payload bytes are the concatenation of all lines strictly between the opening and closing fence lines, each line terminated by `\n` (LF). The opening and closing fence lines themselves are NOT part of the payload. When no closing fence exists (E3), the payload is every line after the opening fence line to the end of `content`.

summary: Multiple matching fenced blocks: first is payload, rest ignored.
text: A patch event's `content` MAY contain multiple fenced blocks. The **first** block (in document order) whose info string matches E2 is the patch payload; all subsequent matching blocks are prose and MUST be ignored as patch payloads.

summary: No matching fenced block → no-op (§4.4).
text: If no fenced block matching E2 is present in `content`, the patch is a no-op (see §4.4, Prose-only and no-op patches).

summary: Prose-only patch is a valid no-op.
text: A prose-only patch event (no fenced `diff` / `patch` block matching E2) is a valid no-op.

summary: Header-only fenced block (valid headers, zero hunks) is a valid no-op.
text: A header-only fenced block (valid `--- a/content` / `+++ b/content` headers, zero hunks) is a valid no-op. Consumers MUST NOT reject this shape as malformed.

summary: Both no-op shapes MUST be treated as successful no-op application.
text: Consumers MUST treat both N1 and N2 as successful no-op application against the current content: the content is unchanged; the event is recorded in the chain as normal.

summary: `---`/`+++` path tokens MUST be exactly `a/content` and `b/content`.
text: The `---` and `+++` header path tokens MUST be exactly `a/content` and `b/content` respectively. A payload with any other path tokens is invalid.

summary: Trailing data on header/`@@` lines leaves a payload valid; tolerate and ignore it.
text: A payload carrying trailing data on its `---`, `+++`, `diff --git`, or `@@` lines (timestamps as emitted by `patch -u` / GNU `diff -u`, whitespace, etc.) **is valid**; consumers MUST tolerate that data and MUST ignore it.

summary: An `Index:` preamble leaves a payload valid; it MAY appear and MUST be tolerated.
text: A payload carrying the `Index:` preamble (capital `I`, followed by an `===…` separator line) **is valid**; the preamble MAY appear and consumers MUST tolerate it. It is *not* the same as the `index <sha>..<sha>` line emitted by `git diff` by default, which is forbidden (see P2).

summary: A `diff --git` line leaves a payload valid; it MAY appear and MUST be tolerated.
text: A payload carrying a `diff --git a/content b/content` line before the headers **is valid**; the line MAY appear and consumers MUST tolerate it. It is not required.

summary: A hunk line beginning with `\` is a no-newline marker; key on the prefix, not the (localised) text.
text: A hunk line beginning with `\` is a no-newline-at-end-of-file marker: it signals the absence of a trailing newline in the corresponding side of the diff, and consumers MUST handle it per the unified-diff spec. Consumers MUST key on the `\` prefix; **the marker's text is informational and MUST NOT be relied upon**, because GNU diff and git translate it through gettext (`\ No newline at end of file` under an English locale, `\ Kein Zeilenumbruch am Dateiende` under `LANG=de_DE.UTF-8`). Matching the English text loses the signal on a payload produced under another locale, which changes the resulting bytes that PB-1 makes normative.

summary: `@@` line numbers advisory; consumers locate hunks by context match.
text: Hunk `@@` line numbers are advisory. Consumers MUST locate each hunk by context match against the current content, subject to the determinism requirement in §5.3.

summary: Floor on acceptance: any payload matching the §5.2 grammar is valid, zero-hunk included; no stricter reading.
text: **Floor on acceptance.** Any patch payload matching the consumer grammar above **is valid**, including one carrying a header block and zero hunks (the header-only no-op shape, N2). A conforming consumer MUST accept every such payload and MUST NOT apply a stricter reading of the grammar than the grammar states. This is the inclusive counterpart to C1: C1 fixes what the valid set excludes, C7 fixes its lower bound. It is what forbids a consumer being stricter than the grammar on its own initiative, a case TR-1's second clause does not reach because no A or D rule is involved.

summary: Multiple file sections permitted; a `---` at hunk-line position starts a section, not a removal.
text: **Multiple file sections.** A payload MAY carry more than one `file-section`. A `---` line occurring where a hunk line could appear begins a new file section; it MUST NOT be interpreted as a removal line. Consumers MUST process the hunks of every section as a single sequence in document order, sequenced per §5.3 T3, and MUST NOT drop any section. Because §5.2 C1 constrains every section's paths to `a/content` / `b/content`, the sections address one and the same content.

summary: Producers SHOULD emit `min(3, available)` context lines; not a validity criterion for consumers.
text: **Context lines.** Producers SHOULD emit `min(3, available)` lines of context before and after each change block — three where the content affords it, and as many as exist where it does not. This is a **producer obligation, enforced when building a patch, not a validity criterion applied to a received one**: `--unified=3` and its equivalents specify a *maximum* the tool supplies where the content affords it, never a minimum it guarantees, and "available" depends on the target event's content, which a validity check over a single event never sees. Consumers MUST NOT reject a payload for carrying fewer context lines; a zero-context hunk is normal (see T2) and the §5.2 example below has none.

summary: No `index <sha>..<sha>`, `mode`, `similarity index`, or rename metadata; `--no-index` does not suppress them.
text: No `index <oldsha>..<newsha> <mode>` lines (the lowercase-`index` form emitted by `git diff` by default), no `mode` lines, no `similarity index` lines, and no rename metadata. Strip these post-hoc. Note that `--no-index` does **not** suppress them — it makes git diff two paths outside a repository and has no effect on index-line emission — so a producer using the `git` invocation recommended above MUST filter the index line itself.

summary: Producers MUST emit UTF-8 with LF line endings in the payload; not a consumer rejection criterion.
text: Producers MUST emit UTF-8 with LF line endings inside the payload. A producer obligation, enforced when building an event: a consumer MUST NOT reject a payload over its line endings, because PB-2 forbids normalising the payload bytes, so a CRLF payload simply fails to match LF content and is handled by the determinism requirement (T1) as an ordinary failure to apply. Rejecting it at the Validity layer instead would pre-empt that with a harsher outcome for the same defect.

summary: Producers SHOULD verify their patch applies cleanly before publishing.
text: Producers SHOULD verify their patch applies cleanly against the target event's resolved content before publishing.

summary: Determinism: context+`-` lines MUST occur exactly once in current content.
text: **Determinism (unambiguous context).** Each hunk's context lines together with its removed (`-`) lines MUST occur exactly once in the current content at the time of application. If the pattern occurs zero times, the patch is invalid (HALT, H1). If the pattern occurs two or more times, the patch is also invalid — the protocol does not rely on the hunk's `@@` line numbers for disambiguation, because production appliers (`git apply`, jsdiff) treat those line numbers as advisory and relocate hunks based on context match. Implementations MAY use the `@@` line numbers as a hint for the initial search position but MUST verify uniqueness across the full target content before applying.

summary: Insertion carve-out: pure-insertion hunks apply at the `@@` `-`-line position, clamped to the content's line range.
text: **Insertion carve-out.** A hunk with no context lines and no `-` lines (e.g., `@@ -0,0 +1,N @@` against empty content, or any pure-insertion hunk) has no pattern to disambiguate. Such a hunk MUST apply at the position implied by its `@@` header's `-` line number; the T1 uniqueness check does not apply. **That line number is interpreted in the coordinates of the patch's pre-application content, and MUST be carried forward by the net line delta of all prior hunks in the same patch.** Without the carry-forward this rule and T3 designate different positions the moment an earlier hunk in the same patch has added or removed lines, and the patch silently produces wrong content; with it, both rules hold simultaneously. This is what `git apply` and jsdiff both do. **If the implied position, after carry-forward, falls outside the current content's line range, it clamps: a position past the last line inserts the `+` lines after the final line, and one before the first line inserts them at the start.** The line count is the count of the content's own lines — a final newline terminates the last line and does not add one, so `a\nb\n` has two lines and a `@@ -3,0 +3,1 @@` hunk against it appends after `b`. Clamping defines the position; it is not a failed match, and it never reaches T1 or invokes H1. C6's context-match remedy cannot supply the missing semantics here — a pure-insertion hunk has no context lines by definition — so without this sentence an out-of-range header would be an input the grammar permits with three defensible dispositions (clamp here, clamp elsewhere, or HALT) and no named one.

summary: Multi-hunk sequencing: each hunk checked against post-prior-hunks content.
text: **Multi-hunk sequencing.** When a patch carries multiple hunks, the T1 check for each hunk is evaluated against the content as produced after all prior hunks in the **same patch** have already been applied. Hunks are processed in document order, across every `file-section` of the payload (C8). A hunk that would satisfy T1 against the pre-patch content but fails after an earlier hunk in the same patch has shifted matching positions causes the patch to HALT (H1). A pure-insertion hunk has no pattern and so is never subject to this check; its position is governed by T2's carry-forward instead.

summary: HALT: pre-validation failure freezes chain at last successful patch.
text: **HALT semantics.** If pre-validation fails for a patch in the canonical chain, the patched content is the state after the last successfully applied patch (or the root state, if the first patch is invalid). No later patches are applied, even if they might themselves be individually valid. HALT is reevaluated whenever the chain topology changes — most commonly when the invalid patch is kind 5 deleted by its author (§10), removing it from the chain.

summary: Invalid patches MUST be surfaced as protocol error annotations.
text: **Protocol error annotation.** Implementations MUST surface an invalid patch as a protocol error annotation, including the event ID, author, and the failure reason.

summary: Canonical chain walks root-author patches via NIP-10 `e reply`.
text: The canonical chain is built by walking root-author patches (those whose `pubkey` equals the root event's `pubkey`) by following NIP-10 `e reply` markers from the root forward. A root-author patch whose `e reply` target is unobserved contributes no position to the walk; it is held per UR-4 until re-evaluated on the target's arrival.

summary: Kind 5 cascade applied during chain build.
text: Kind 5 cascade per §10 is applied while building the chain (deleted patches and their descendants are removed).

summary: Foreign patches never enter the canonical chain; same T/H rules apply to overlays.
text: Foreign patches (those whose `pubkey` differs from the root event's `pubkey`) never enter the canonical chain. They are evaluated separately as overlays against their `e reply` target's resolved content (the target-state snapshot rule, §7.3). The same T1/T2/T3/H1 rules apply when computing an overlay's classification against its target.

summary: Producers SHOULD respect the recommended resource bounds of §5.4.
text: Producers SHOULD respect the recommended bounds of §5.4.

summary: Consumers SHOULD enforce configurable ceilings and bound total patch-application work in bytes compared, with a per-line floor on the match pattern.
text: Consumers SHOULD enforce configurable ceilings and SHOULD bound total patch-application work (bytes compared, charged at no less than one unit per line of the hunk's match pattern (T1)), not only hunk or patch counts.

summary: Ceiling exceeded → resource-limit-exceeded annotation, never HALT; event remains V-valid.
text: Exceeding a ceiling aborts application and MUST be surfaced as a distinct resource-limit-exceeded annotation, never as HALT. The event remains V-valid.

summary: Content abandoned for resource reasons MUST NOT be served or cached as canonical bytes.
text: Content abandoned for resource reasons MUST NOT be served or cached as canonical bytes.

summary: A chain stopped by a ceiling is *aborted under a ceiling* — distinct from both resolved and HALT.
text: **Chain disposition under a ceiling.** A chain whose application was stopped by a ceiling is reported as **aborted under a ceiling**, distinct from both `resolved` and HALT. Reporting it as `resolved` would name the last applied patch as the tip and claim a completeness the implementation does not have — which RC-3 then obliges non-UI consumers to serve downstream. Reporting it as HALT is forbidden by RL-3. The report MUST identify the patch at which application stopped and the ceiling that was reached, and MUST NOT cite H1.

summary: V-invalid events MUST NOT enter SCRUTINY processing; V-valid events MUST NOT be rejected by an A or D rule.
text: V-invalid events MUST NOT enter SCRUTINY processing and MUST NOT be rendered. A V-valid event MUST NOT be rejected by an A or D rule (§6.0).

summary: Event admitted if `pubkey` trusted OR reachable via a trusted Binding.
text: A SCRUTINY event is admitted to a user's view if its `pubkey` is trusted OR it is reachable via a trusted Binding (§6.2).

summary: Binding admitted only if its `pubkey` is trusted; no transitive endpoint trust.
text: A Binding event is admitted only if its `pubkey` is trusted. Trust does NOT flow transitively through the endpoints (§6.3).

summary: A trusted Binding admits its `e root` and `e link` endpoints, until the Binding is retracted.
text: When a Binding is admitted, both of its endpoints (`e root` and `e link`) become reachable and are admitted even if their authors are not directly trusted (§6.4) — for as long as the Binding is not retracted (§10, DEL-5).

summary: Root admission admits the root's canonical chain, for as long as the root's admission survives.
text: When a root Product or Metadata is admitted, its canonical chain is admitted with it: root-author patches and root-author kind 5 events targeting them are admitted automatically — for as long as the root's own admission survives (§10, DEL-5).

summary: Foreign patches are NOT transitively admitted; require independent trust.
text: Foreign patches are NOT transitively admitted via root admission. They require independent trust on the foreign author's pubkey.

summary: Trust filtering is presentation-time; MUST NOT precede chain construction, self-fork detection, or overlay classification.
text: Trust filtering is applied at presentation time, to the results of chain and overlay computation. Implementations MUST NOT filter by trust before canonical-chain construction, self-fork detection, or overlay classification.

summary: Canonical chain = linear root-author patch sequence by `e reply`.
text: The canonical chain is the linear sequence of patch events whose `pubkey` equals the root event's `pubkey`, threaded by NIP-10 `e reply` markers from the root forward.

summary: Canonical bytes computed from root + canonical chain; overlays excluded.
text: Canonical bytes are computed strictly from the root event plus the canonical chain. Foreign overlays are NOT part of canonical bytes.

summary: Non-UI consumers MUST recompute on observed-set change.
text: Non-UI consumers MUST recompute canonical bytes and overlay states whenever their observed event set changes in a way that affects events they serve.

summary: UI consumers SHOULD recompute on observed-set change.
text: UI consumers SHOULD recompute on observed-set change.

summary: The tip is the last chain event — the root itself where the chain carries no patches.
text: **Tip identification.** The tip is the last event in the canonical chain: the last patch where the chain carries patches, and the root event itself where it carries none. An unresolved self-fork leaves the chain undefined (SF-1) and the tip undefined with it. This matters because §7.3's `clean` classification turns on whether the overlay's target *is* the tip: reading the tip as "the last patch" and nothing else makes an overlay on a root that has never been patched `stale`, asserting that the chain has advanced past a target it has not advanced past. That is the first annotation published against any new Product, so it is the common case.

summary: Root self-fork: two root-author patches at same parent → chain undefined; a shared pending parent holds both (UR-4), no fork yet.
text: A **root self-fork** occurs when two or more root-author patches reply to the same parent event. The canonical chain is undefined while the self-fork is unresolved. Two patches sharing a parent that is itself held pending an unobserved target (UR-4) are not a fork: neither participates in the chain yet, so there is no position to contend for, and detection re-evaluates if and when the target arrives.

summary: Freeze patched content at shared parent while unresolved.
text: Clients MUST freeze the patched content at the shared parent of the forked patches while the self-fork is unresolved.

summary: Surface self-fork as an explicit error condition.
text: Clients MUST surface the self-fork as an explicit error condition (event IDs of both branches, timestamps, available context).

summary: MUST NOT pick branch by `created_at`, event ID, or any heuristic.
text: Clients MUST NOT silently pick one branch by `created_at`, event ID, or any other heuristic.

summary: Resolution: root author kind 5 deletion on one branch.
text: Resolution: the root author emits a kind 5 deletion targeting a patch in one of the forked branches; topology cascade (§10) eliminates that branch in its entirety.

summary: Multiple forks resolved independently; freeze at earliest unresolved.
text: Multiple unresolved forks are resolved independently; patched content is frozen at the earliest unresolved fork.

summary: Self-fork vs HALT: freeze at whichever is earlier in chain order; never apply past a HALT.
text: **Precedence between a self-fork and a HALT.** Where a self-fork (SF-2) and a HALT (§5.3 H1) are both live, canonical bytes freeze at whichever point is earlier in chain order. A self-fork upstream of a HALT freezes at the shared parent, and the patches downstream of it — including the one that would have HALTed — are never evaluated, because the chain past an undefined point is not evaluated at all. A HALT upstream of a self-fork freezes at the last successfully applied patch; the fork is still surfaced per SF-3 though it did not determine the content. Implementations MUST NOT apply any patch past a HALT in order to reach a downstream fork parent: H1 admits no exception, and doing so would return different canonical bytes for the same event set than an implementation that did not.

summary: *Reserved.* See **PT-7** (§4.4).
text: *Reserved.* Foreign-patch reply-target validity is normative under **PT-7** (§4.4). This ID is retained for cross-reference stability.

summary: Target-state snapshot: overlay evaluated against target's resolved content.
text: **Target-state snapshot.** An overlay is interpreted against the target's resolved content — the canonical bytes computed by applying the canonical chain up to and including the foreign patch's `e reply` target. This is the byte sequence the overlay author signed against, and the only sequence the overlay is evaluated against.

summary: Undefined target content → overlay is orphaned, not clean/conflict/stale.
text: If the overlay's `e reply` target has no defined resolved content (downstream of HALT, inside an unresolved self-fork, itself a sibling in such a fork, or held pending an unobserved reply parent per UR-4), the overlay MUST be treated as **orphaned** and MUST NOT be classified as clean / conflict / stale.

summary: Classification is a pure deterministic function of (payload, target content).
text: Overlay classification against its target is a pure function of (overlay payload, target's resolved content) and MUST be deterministic across compliant clients. Given fixed ceilings, this holds for OV-9's `unclassified` outcome too; because ceilings are local and configurable (RL-2), two clients with *different* ceilings MAY reach different outcomes, and that is the one permitted source of divergence.

summary: Clients SHOULD expose classification through their API/data layer.
text: Clients SHOULD expose the classification (clean / conflict / stale / orphaned, or `unclassified` per OV-9) through their API/data layer so downstream tooling can read it. Visual rendering remains client-defined.

summary: Overlay rendered against original target; "rebase preview" is non-normative.
text: A foreign overlay is rendered against its original `e reply` target's resolved content. Clients MAY additionally offer a "rebase preview" against the current canonical tip; this is informational and outside the protocol's normative surface.

summary: Foreign overlay visible only if its `pubkey` is in the user's trusted set.
text: A foreign patch is visible to the user only if its `pubkey` is in the user's trusted set. The trust set gates which overlays appear; it does not affect the canonical chain.

summary: Root-author patch replying to foreign patch ignored for chain construction.
text: A root-author patch whose `e reply` points at a foreign patch is ignored for canonical-chain construction.

summary: Ceiling reached before classification → `unclassified`; never conflict, orphaned, clean or stale.
text: **Ceiling reached before classification.** If a §5.4 consumer ceiling is reached while classifying an overlay, the outcome is **unclassified** — a distinct fifth outcome, not one of the four classifications. Such an overlay MUST NOT be reported as `conflict` (no failure was established), as `orphaned` (the target is well defined and obtainable, and the α/β rule does not apply), or as `clean` or `stale` (the hunks were never shown to apply). It MUST be accompanied by the distinct resource-limit-exceeded annotation of RL-3, and MUST NOT cite H1.

summary: Ingestion MUST be confluent: state depends on the observed set, never on arrival order.
text: Ingestion MUST be confluent: the state an implementation reaches depends only on the set of events observed, never on arrival order.

summary: Patch with unobserved `e root` is retained and re-evaluated on the root's arrival.
text: A Patch whose `e root` is unobserved MUST be retained and re-evaluated on the root's arrival. It does not participate in the canonical chain until then.

summary: Classification cached as permanent only when no further observation could change it.
text: A classification MAY be cached as permanent only when no further observation could change it. A Patch's authorship class MUST NOT be cached while its root is unobserved.

summary: Root-author patch with unobserved `e reply` target is retained and re-evaluated on arrival; no chain or fork participation until then.
text: A root-author patch whose `e reply` target is unobserved MUST be retained and re-evaluated on the target's arrival. It does not participate in canonical-chain construction or self-fork detection until then; PT-6 is evaluated if and when the target is observed.

summary: Discovery queries assume NIP-01 `#t`/`#e`/`#i` filters; include `#t:["scrutiny-fabric"]`.
text: All discovery queries assume relays supporting NIP-01 `#t`, `#e`, and `#i` filters and MUST include `#t:["scrutiny-fabric"]` (except for kind 5 lookups, which do not carry `scrutiny-fabric` tags).

summary: SHOULD issue `{kinds:[5], #e:[<id>]}` per cached root, patch, and Binding, periodically.
text: Clients SHOULD issue `{kinds:[5], #e:[<id>]}` for every chain root, every patch, and every Binding they cache, both at first sight and periodically thereafter, to guard against relays that store deletions but omit them from default filter results. Binding deletions are required because retraction revokes conferred admission (§10, DEL-5).

summary: NIP-50 search results MUST be verified for valid `scrutiny-fabric` tags and intent match.
text: When falling back to NIP-50 free-text `search` queries (§8.1 step 3), clients MUST verify returned events carry valid `scrutiny-fabric` tags (per §3) and match the user's intent. NIP-50 ranking is relay-dependent and untrusted.

summary: `{"#e":[id]}` traversal results MUST be filtered for the expected `scrutiny-*` `t` tag and `e` markers inspected for role.
text: When traversing `e`-tag references via `{"#e":[<event-id>]}` (§4.3, §8.2), results MUST be filtered for the expected `scrutiny-*` event-type `t` tag, and the `e` tag markers (`root`, `link`, `reply`) MUST be inspected to determine each result's role relative to the queried event.

summary: `i` prefix is lowercase ASCII matching `[a-z0-9-]+`.
text: Prefix is lowercase ASCII matching `[a-z0-9-]+`.

summary: `i` value is the source authority's canonical form, preserved verbatim.
text: Value is the source authority's canonical form, preserved verbatim (case, punctuation, separators all as the issuing body writes them).

summary: Parsers split on the first `:` only.
text: Parsers split on the **first** `:` only; values containing colons (e.g., `cpe:2.3:...`) work transparently.

summary: Unknown prefixes valid; pass through as opaque indexers.
text: Unknown prefixes are valid; parsers pass them through and treat them as opaque indexers.

summary: Kind 5 honored only when `pubkey` matches target event's `pubkey`.
text: A kind 5 deletion is honored only when its `pubkey` matches the target event's `pubkey`.

summary: Root-author patch deletion → topology cascade in canonical chain.
text: Deletion of a root-author patch removes the patch and all its canonical descendants from the canonical chain (topology cascade). The patched content reverts to the last surviving ancestor.

summary: Foreign overlay deletion → hidden from default; canonical bytes unaffected.
text: Deletion of a foreign overlay hides it from default overlay rendering. Canonical bytes are unaffected.

summary: Root deletion → default-view retraction; annotations preserved for audit.
text: Deletion of a root Product/Metadata hides the root from default views. The canonical chain, foreign overlays, and Bindings referencing the root are preserved for audit. Clients MUST NOT silently drop annotations or patches associated with a retracted root.

summary: Binding deletion → edge retraction and revocation of the admission it conferred; endpoints stay V-valid.
text: Deletion of a Binding hides the edge from default views **and revokes the admission it conferred** (TR-4). Endpoints remain V-valid and are never cascade-deleted; an endpoint with no surviving admission path leaves the default view along with its canonical chain. An independently-admitted overlay whose target has left the view renders per the α/β rule, not dropped.

summary: Kind 5 events cannot themselves be kind-5-deleted.
text: A kind 5 event cannot itself be deleted by another kind 5 event. To restore previously deleted content, the author must publish a fresh event with a new ID.

summary: α/β degradation for orphaned overlays; not re-anchored.
text: **α/β degradation for orphaned overlays.** If the overlay's target is obtainable (cached or fetched), render against the target's universe (α). If unobtainable, render as a standalone artifact (β); the overlay is not re-anchored to any other event.

summary: Late-arriving deletion target → retroactive application; recompute content.
text: If a kind 5 deletion's target is not yet available, the deletion event is recorded and applied retroactively once the target becomes available. Patched content MUST be recomputed when a previously-unavailable deletion target arrives.

summary: MUST cache received kind 5 events and apply during chain construction.
text: Implementations MUST cache locally received kind 5 deletion events and apply them during chain construction, regardless of whether the queried relay reports the deletion.

summary: Clients SHOULD offer a "show deleted events" toggle exposing deleted events + descendants.
text: Clients SHOULD offer a "show deleted events" toggle that, when enabled, surfaces deleted events and all their descendants (patches against a deleted root, overlays against deleted patches, etc.) so users can inspect the historical state.

summary: SCRUTINY-aware relays SHOULD store kind 5 deletions targeting scrutiny-fabric events alongside originals.
text: SCRUTINY-aware relays SHOULD inspect the `e` tag target of a kind 5 event; if the target event carries a `scrutiny-fabric` `t` tag, the relay SHOULD store the deletion alongside the original and surface it to SCRUTINY-aware queriers.
